claim: The economy is rigged against working people
label: narrative
summary: Originated from Multiple co-originators: Joseph E. Stiglitz (academic formalization), Bernie Sanders (political popularization), Elizabeth Warren (Senate amplification); the framing itself has roots in labor and left-populist rhetoric dating to the mid-20th century and earlier (circa 2011-2016 (modern popularization); Stiglitz Scientific American article ~2019). The 'rigged economy' framing gained modern traction through Bernie Sanders' 2016 presidential campaign rhetoric and Elizabeth Warren's Senate messaging, was academically formalized by Nobel laureate Joseph Stiglitz in Scientific American (~2019), then amplified by labor unions (AFT), polling organizations (Ipsos confirming 69% public agreement by 2023), economics blogs, and social media. Conservative and libertarian critics (Mises Institute, Hoover Institution, National Affairs) pushed back, inadvertently amplifying the framing further. Trump's parallel use of 'rigged system' language (directed at political elites rather than economic inequality) cross-pollinated the phrase across ideological lines.. The modern 'economy is rigged against working people' framing was popularized primarily through Bernie Sanders' 2015-2016 presidential campaign and Elizabeth Warren's ongoing Senate messaging, drawing on a much older populist and labor tradition traceable to Marx and mid-century labor movements. Nobel laureate Joseph Stiglitz provided academic credibility with his Scientific American article arguing that post-1970s rule changes systematically advantaged the wealthy. The narrative spread organically across labor organizations, mainstream polling, and social media, though critics at outlets like National Affairs and the Hoover Institution argue the 'rigged' framing oversimplifies complex structural economic shifts and lacks evidence of coordinated elite intent.

primary_source.title: Joseph E. Stiglitz (Nobel laureate economist), published in Scientific American
primary_source.excerpt: Since the mid-1970s the rules of the economic game have been rewritten, both globally and nationally, in ways that advantage the rich and disadvantage the rest... This is not only because of the shift to a service-sector economy—it is because of the rigged rules of the game, rules set in a political system that is itself rigged through gerrymandering, voter suppression and the influence of money.
